ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
Two small sliders A and B, each with mass $m$, are connected by a light rope and placed on an inclined plane with an angle $\theta = 37^{\circ}$. A constant horizontal force $F$ is applied to slider B to the right, and both sliders are just on the verge of not sliding upwards. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the sliders and the inclined plane is $\mu = 0.5$, and the maximum static friction is equal to the kinetic friction. It is known that $\sin 37^{\circ} = 0.6$, and the gravitational acceleration is $g$.

1. What is the magnitude of the tension force exerted by the light rope on block A?
2. What is the magnitude of the external force $F$?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The diagram shows an inclined plane rising to the right with angle 37° marked at the base. Slider A is lower on the plane and slider B is higher on the same plane; they are connected by a light rope along the incline. A horizontal force F points to the right on slider B. Reasoning following the free-body method: Since the sliders are just on the verge of moving upward along the incline, friction on each slider acts down the incline and has limiting magnitude μN. For block A, the normal force is N_A = mg cosθ. Along the incline, tension T pulls A upward, while gravity component mg sinθ and friction μmg cosθ act downward. Equilibrium gives T = mg sinθ + μmg cosθ. With sin37° = 0.6, cos37° = 0.8, and μ = 0.5, T = mg(0.6) + 0.5mg(0.8) = 0.6mg + 0.4mg = mg. For block B, the horizontal force has component F cosθ up the incline and component F sinθ into the plane, so N_B = mg cosθ + F sinθ. Along the incline, the upward component F cosθ balances tension T, gravity component mg sinθ, and friction μN_B downward: F cosθ = T + mg sinθ + μN_B. Substituting N_B and T = mg: F(0.8) = mg + 0.6mg + 0.5(0.8mg + 0.6F). Thus 0.8F = 2.0mg + 0.3F, so 0.5F = 2mg and F = 4mg.
